extracted.intended_audience: Researchers preparing NSF grant proposals and prospective NSF peer reviewers / program officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the NSF merit review process for proposal preparation, peer review, reviewer selection/conflicts, return-without-review conditions, funding decisions, and feedback to proposers.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Science Board Approved Merit Review Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the intellectual merit of the proposed activity? What are the broader impacts of the proposed activity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the two primary review criteria; program-specific criteria as stated in the program solicitation also apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential considerations include: How important is the proposed activity to advancing knowledge and understanding within its own field or across different fields? How well qualified is the proposer (individual or team) to conduct the project? To what extent does the proposed activity suggest and explore creative and original concepts? How well conceived and organized is the proposed activity? Is there sufficient access to resources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should comment on the quality of prior work if appropriate. Evaluate significance, qualifications, creativity/originality, design/organization, and access to resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential considerations include: How well does the activity advance discovery and understanding while promoting teaching, training and learning? How well does the activity broaden the participation of underrepresented groups? To what extent will it enhance the infrastructure for research and education, such as facilities, instrumentation, networks and partnerships? Will the results be disseminated broadly to enhance scientific and technological understanding? What may be the benefits of the proposed activity to society?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See linked examples (http://www.nsf.gov/pubs/gpg/broaderimpacts.pdf). Reviewers should weigh effects on education/training, diversity/broadening participation, infrastructure enhancement, dissemination plans, and societal benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts — Examples (teaching, training, learning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate research activities into the teaching of science, math and engineering at all educational levels; include students (K-12, undergraduate, non-science majors, graduate) as participants; participate in recruitment/training/professional development of K-12 teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these activities as concrete evidence of broader impacts when appropriate; additional examples available at the Broader Impacts guidance link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts — Examples (broaden participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish research and education collaborations with students and/or faculty who are members of underrepresented groups; include students from underrepresented groups; establish collaborations with non-Ph.D.-granting institutions and those serving underrepresented groups; make campus visits and presentations at institutions that serve underrepresented groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate clear plans and activities that will broaden participation; include specific populations and partnership strategies where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts — Examples (enhance infrastructure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and establish collaborations between disciplines and institutions, among U.S. academic institutions, industry and government and with international partners; stimulate development and dissemination of next-generation instrumentation, multi-user facilities, and shared research/education platforms; maintain/operate/modernize shared research and education infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how proposed work will develop or sustain infrastructure and multi-user resources, and identify partners and dissemination channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts — Examples (broad dissemination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partner with museums, nature centers, science centers to develop exhibits; involve the public or industry in research and education activities; give public presentations (museums, libraries, radio); make data available in a timely manner via databases or digital libraries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dissemination plans and public engagement activities, and specify mechanisms and timelines for data sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts — Examples (benefits to society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate linkage between discovery and societal benefit with specific examples; partner with federal agencies and private sector to integrate research into broader programs; analyze and synthesize results for non-scientists; provide information to policy makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain practical applications and societal benefits clearly, and describe formats tailored for non-specialist audiences and policy use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return Without Review — Project Summary requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Per Important Notice 127, proposals that do not separately address both criteria within the one-page Project Summary will be returned without review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the one-page Project Summary contains distinct statements addressing Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts; failure to do so leads to immediate return without review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return Without Review — Other grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals may be returned without review if: inappropriate for funding by NSF; submitted with insufficient lead-time before activity begins; a full proposal submitted after receiving a 'not invited' for a preliminary proposal; duplicate or substantially similar to a proposal already under consideration; does not meet proposal preparation requirements (page limits, formatting, electronic submission); not responsive to GPG or program solicitation; misses announced deadline; previously reviewed and declined and not substantially revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully follow the Grant Proposal Guide and program solicitation requirements and timelines; substantially revise previously declined proposals before resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Selection — types and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of reviewers recruited: reviewers with specialized knowledge, reviewers with broad/generalized knowledge, and diverse representation within the review group. Sources include program officer's knowledge, references listed in the proposal, recent professional society programs, computer searches of S&E journal articles related to the proposal, and reviewer recommendations included in the proposal or sent by email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposers may suggest well-qualified reviewers and identify persons they prefer not to review their proposal; suggestions are invited but final selection rests with NSF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Conflicts of Interest (procedures and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary purpose is to remove or limit influence of ties to an applicant institution or investigator that could affect reviewer advice; second purpose is to preserve trust in integrity and evenhandedness of NSF's process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of affiliations: current employment at the institution, other employment such as consultant, being considered for employment, office or board membership. Examples of relationships: family/marriage, business partner, past/present thesis advisor or student, collaboration within last 48 months, co-editing within last 24 months. Reviewers with such ties are handled per conflict procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Peer Reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Review all proposal materials and consider the two NSF merit review criteria and any program specific criteria; evaluate adequacy of proposed project plan including budget, resources, & timeline; consider program & field priorities and potential risks and benefits of the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make independent written comments on the quality of the proposal content. Each proposal gets at least three individual peer reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Peer Review Panel
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the merits of the proposal with other panelists who reviewed the proposal; write a summary proposal review based on discussion; make a panel recommendation to NSF on whether the proposal should be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels may be supplemented with ad hoc reviewers if additional expertise is needed; panel summaries and recommendations guide program officer decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Ad Hoc Review; Panel Review; Ad Hoc plus Panel Review; Internal Review Only (e.g., SGERs). Also panels of program officers, less formally assembled sets of program officers, and individual program officers conduct reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that review modality varies by program and solicitation; the number and type of reviews influences the feedback and recommendation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding Decision Process and Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review panel summary provides review and a recommendation on funding and feedback. NSF Program Officers make funding recommendations guided by program goals and portfolio considerations. NSF Division Directors concur or reject program officer recommendations. NSF grants and agreements officers make the official award considering issues such as institutional grant management capacity, overdue reports, and other outstanding issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A positive panel recommendation does not guarantee an award; institutional administrative and compliance factors are considered at award stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for Funding a Competitive Proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors include likely high impact; special programmatic fit; PI career point (tenured/established/young); place in program portfolio; other support for PI; impact on institution/state (CAREER/RUI/EPSCoR); diversity issues; educational impact; whether the proposal is launching versus maintaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic balance, portfolio needs, and broader institutional and educational impacts can influence selection among otherwise competitive proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for Declining a Proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal was not considered competitive by the peer review panel and the program office concurred; the proposal had flaws or issues identified by the program office; program funds were not adequate to fund all competitive proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviews, panel summaries, and program officer comments become available via FastLane after decisions; use feedback to improve future competitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback to PI — Documentation and Ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation from merit review includes verbatim copies of individual reviews (excluding reviewer identities in most cases), panel summary (if panel reviewed), context statement, and PO to PI comments as necessary. Information includes reviewer ratings (E, VG, G, F, P), analysis of how well proposal addresses Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts, and proposal strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposers have questions about feedback, they should contact the cognizant program officer. Use the feedback to determine whether and how to revise before resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Should you revise and resubmit? Consider whether reviewers and the PO identify significant strengths; whether you can address the weaknesses identified; and whether colleagues can suggest other ways to strengthen a resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the cognizant program officer with questions; substantial revision is expected if resubmitting a previously declined proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Makes a Successful Proposal (high-level advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address all the proposal review criteria; understand the NSF peer review process; avoid common omissions and mistakes; encourage faculty who write grants to serve as NSF peer reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early and frequent contact with program officers is encouraged ('Ask Early, Ask Often!'). Serving as a reviewer helps learn common problems and strategies to write strong proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Become a Peer Reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact the NSF program officer(s) of relevant programs: introduce yourself and your research experience; tell them you want to become a peer reviewer; ask when the next panel will be held; offer to send a 2-page CV with current contact information; stay in touch if you don’t hear back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive outreach to program officers and maintaining updated CV/contact info increases chances of participation as a reviewer.
